title: Mets’ sell-off continues as Clay Holmes, Tyrone Taylor dealt to Cubs
content:
The Athletic has live coverage of the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline.

CHICAGO — Jed Hoyer doesn’t love the phrase “all-in” when it comes to acquiring players. But a flurry of moves over 24 hours, which has seen him send away some of his top prospects, suggests he’s not taking the 2026 season for granted. Already having acquired Kevin Gausman for the rotation, the Cubs made a deal with the New York Mets to add veteran starter Clay Holmes and right-handed outfielder Tyrone Taylor, a league source told The Athletic.

The cost was high as the Cubs sent infield prospect Jefferson Rojas, arguably their current top prospect, to the Mets. Giving up Rojas for two rentals is not something the Cubs front office normally does, but their behavior suggests the Cubs believe this team has what it takes to make a deep run in the playoffs.

The Mets, meanwhile, continued their sell-off.  Holmes has not pitched since mid-May after getting struck by a comebacker that fractured his right fibula. Since he is close to a return and the injury had nothing to do with his arm, teams were pursuing him in the trade market. Holmes, 33, holds a player option for 2027 worth $12 million.

Holmes made an impressive transition from high-leverage reliever to dependable starter. Ahead of the 2025 season, the Mets signed Holmes to a three-year, $38 million guarantee with the plan to immediately convert the former Yankees closer into a starter.

The first year went well. Holmes made 31 starts, plus two other appearances, and racked up 165 2/3 innings, a considerable jump after not exceeding 70 innings in any of the prior four seasons. He had a 3.53 ERA and 1.304 WHIP. At times, he showed some fatigue in the second half of the season and sometimes struggled with his command.

Holmes’ 2026 season got off to a fantastic start. Over nine starts, Holmes holds a 2.39 ERA. At the time of his injury, Holmes led the Mets in innings. Teammates and coaches described the loss as a crushing blow because of how much Holmes meant to the team both on and off the field.

Taylor is a prototypical fourth outfielder, capable of playing all three positions well and of putting together a solid at-bat. After a prolonged slump, his offense has really taken off of late. Since returning from the injured list in late June, Taylor has seven home runs in just 48 at-bats, posting a .354/.435/.875/1.311 slash line in that time. It’s looked like he’s changed his leg kick, allowing him to launch pitches on the inner half in the air more consistently. Even if that level of production doesn’t continue, Taylor is a useful piece and much-appreciated clubhouse presence.

The prospect in the deal, Rojas, 21, had a 114 wRC+ at Double A this season. And while he may not stick at shortstop, he is seen as either the Cubs’ No. 1 or No. 2 prospect in a system filled with position-player talent.

Clearly, the Cubs felt comfortable dealing from a position of depth. They have numerous other bats in the system they like, even after dealing Rojas and C/DH Moisés Ballesteros in a separate deal. They also have an infield that’s set for years with Alex Bregman, Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner and Michael Busch. The presence of Matt Shaw (on the IL with a wrist issue) and emergence of Pedro Ramírez as a versatile defender and trusted offensive performer likely made Rojas all the more expendable.

Holmes, who has made two rehab starts, should fit well in the Cubs rotation. The veteran lefty has a career 62 percent groundball rate, which should fare well in front of a Cubs infield defense widely considered the best in baseball.

Taylor upgrades a Cubs bench that has been strong this season but has lacked a consistent right-handed performer. Ramírez has been strong, but still unproven. Michael Conforto has been great off the bench, but is a left-handed hitter. Taylor has a 116 wRC+ overall on the season, but crushes lefties with a 146 wRC+ on the season. The Cubs already have a league-best 119 wRC+ against lefties, but more depth and options for manager Craig Counsell won’t hurt.
